summary: Instrumented the append side - the discriminator the last gap named - and the draft-side run names the proposer state behind the rejected history. For seed 35 the joint-entering change at index 4, term 2 was appended by node 2 in the same step as the first rejection (step 22) with pending_conf_index_before=2, applied_before=3, joint_before=false and validation_disabled=false. Two things follow. The ordinary reading holds: both guard clauses were false in the normal way - alreadyPending was false because pendingConfIndex (2) did not exceed applied (3), and alreadyJoint was false because the appender's tracker was not joint; every other append in the run shows the same shape, including appenders that had applied a dozen entries. But those operands conflict with the history the rejecting nodes hold: if node 2 had applied three entries of a log whose index 2 is a joint-enter change, its tracker would be joint, so either node 2's own entries differ from the log the others applied - a divergence the sweep's invariants would not flag, since they compare committed (index, term) only at check points and only against the value first observed - or the harness produced a tracker state its log does not imply, with the restart path a plausible source, since it rebuilds a node with the ConfState its tracker currently has while its log may already contain a joint change it has not applied. That is exactly why the defect claim stays unresolved rather than asserted, and I recorded the operands as behaviour knowledge pending a receipt, together with the next operand that would settle it: node 2's own entry types and terms for indices 1..4 at the moment of the append, which would show whether its log diverged or its tracker was rebuilt. The consequence chain - in-order application of a joint-enter change while joint is rejected and applyConfChange panics - remains documented, but its reachability through permitted operations is still the open question rather than an established trigger.
